questions.q: 本文の内容に合うものを1つ選びなさい。
choices: a) Leakey's remark was intended to suggest that chimpanzees deserved the same legal status as humans.
b) Before 1960, the ability to make tools was widely regarded as a trait found only in human beings.
c) It was Goodall herself who first proposed that the definition of "man" should be changed.
questions.explain: b は「many scientists believed that making and using tools was what set human beings apart」の言い換え。a は本文が否定、c は定義の変更を口にしたのは Leakey（人物のすり替え）。
questions.passage: In 1960, a young Jane Goodall watched a chimpanzee she had named David Greybeard strip the leaves off a twig, push it into a termite mound, and pull it out covered with insects. At the time, many scientists believed that making and using tools was what set human beings apart from all other animals. When Goodall reported what she had seen, her mentor Louis Leakey famously replied, "Now we must redefine 'tool,' redefine 'man,' or accept chimpanzees as humans." Leakey was not, of course, proposing that chimps be given human rights; he was pointing out that a definition many people had taken for granted no longer held.

questions.q: 対話の内容に合うものを1つ選びなさい。
choices: a) Mika suspects that the videos are made endless so that users will not notice a hidden fee.
b) Ryan argues that attention differs from oil and water in that it can never run out.
c) In Ryan's view, it is in a sense the users themselves that social media companies are selling.
questions.explain: c は "If you're not paying for the product, you are the product." の言い換え。a の hidden fee は本文にない。b は just as easy to exhaust と逆。
questions.passage:
Mika : I don't understand why social media is free. Those companies make billions of dollars every year.
Ryan : There's a saying: "If you're not paying for the product, you are the product." They sell advertisers our attention — every second we spend scrolling is something they can sell.
Mika : So the longer I stay on the app, the more money they make. No wonder the videos never seem to end.
Ryan : Exactly. And that's why some people say our attention has become a natural resource, just like oil or water — and just as easy to exhaust.

questions.q: 本文の内容に合うものを1つ選びなさい。
choices: a) Thoreau used the expression in connection with a preference for simplicity of which he disapproved.
b) The publisher chose the phrase mainly because it had only recently been coined.
c) Young people tend to avoid the term because they regard it as an insult.
questions.explain: a は「criticizing his society for valuing simple ideas over complex ones」の言い換え。b は the expression is not new と矛盾。c は with a sense of humor と逆。
questions.passage: In 2024, Oxford University Press chose "brain rot" as its Word of the Year. The phrase describes the supposed decline of a person's mental state that comes from consuming too much trivial online content. Interestingly, the expression is not new: the American writer Henry David Thoreau used it in 1854, criticizing his society for valuing simple ideas over complex ones. What has changed, according to the publisher, is how often people now use the term — and the fact that young people themselves use it, often with a sense of humor, to describe their own habits.

questions.q: 対話の内容に合うものを1つ選びなさい。
choices: a) The toads were introduced because Australia's native predators were unable to eat them.
b) Although the toads did not multiply as much as expected, they kept the beetles under control.
c) Hiro is reminded of a case in which human action against one species led to unforeseen trouble.
questions.explain: c は「rabbits and foxes の話のようだ」＝人間が1つの種に手を加えて予期せぬ問題が起きた例を連想している。a は持ち込んだ理由のすり替え、b は bred so quickly と逆。
questions.passage:
Ms. Sato : In 1935, about a hundred cane toads were brought from Hawaii to Australia to eat the beetles that were damaging sugar cane.
Hiro : Did it work?
Ms. Sato : Not at all. The toads hardly ate the beetles, but they bred so quickly that there are now estimated to be more than 200 million of them. Because they are poisonous, many native predators that try to eat them die.
Hiro : That sounds like the story of the rabbits and foxes in Jane Goodall's interview.
